title: The Easter vigil
hook: a fire, a great candle, and an ancient song, the Exsultet: this is the night

segments.voice: Yesterday, Holy Saturday: broken gates underfoot, and Adam and Eve pulled up by the wrists. Your line was he pulls them out.

Saturday night, after dark, and the church is pitch black. Outside the door a small fire burns, and people stand around it in their coats. A tall candle is lit from the fire and carried in, and a voice sings out: the light of Christ. The people answer: thanks be to God. The flame is passed from the tall candle, hand to hand, until the dark room is full of small lights. Then someone sings an old song called the Exsultet, and one line keeps coming back in it. This is the night. Today, the Easter vigil.

A vigil is a night spent awake, waiting. This one waits for Easter, and it starts in the dark on purpose. The Exsultet opens by calling heaven and earth to rejoice. Then it turns into a list, and line after line begins: this is the night. This is the night, it sings, when God brought Israel out of Egypt and through the sea. This is the night when a pillar of fire drove back the darkness. This is the night when Christ broke the chains of death and rose. The song reaches back to Exodus, which says of the night Israel left Egypt, in the King James: "It is a night to be much observed unto the LORD for bringing them out from the land of Egypt." Jewish families keep that night at the Passover table with their own telling of the story. The vigil takes up the same night and sets the empty tomb inside it. Then the Exsultet says something daring. It calls Adam's sin a happy fault, because of the rescue it led to: yesterday's icon, sung. After the song, in churches that keep the full vigil, story after story from the Hebrew Bible is read by candlelight: creation, the sea, the prophets. Then the church fills with light. In churches that set the alleluia aside for Lent, it comes back tonight. Some churches baptize new Christians at this service. And the candle carries a line from John's Gospel into the room: "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not."

Turn off as many lights as you can and light one candle somewhere safe, or use the smallest light you have. Watch how far one small flame reaches, the edges of the room you can and can't see. If you pray, say the vigil's line quietly, this is the night; if not, simply stay with the one light and the dark around it.
Exsultet. The ancient song sung by candlelight at the Easter vigil, repeating this is the night as it tells the story of rescue.
Your line: this is the night. One flame, then a room full. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans and some other churches keep the Easter Vigil on Saturday night: a new fire, the Easter candle carried into the dark church, the Exsultet sung, readings from the Hebrew Bible, and sometimes baptisms.

chat.says: Why does the Easter vigil talk so much about Israel leaving Egypt?
options: The Exsultet holds both on one night: the sea crossed, and Christ rising.
The songs were first written for Passover and kept by mistake.
Because the vigil retells Jesus's flight into Egypt as a baby.
chat.meaning: This is the night, the Exsultet sings: when God brought Israel through the sea, and when Christ broke the chains of death and rose.

notes: The Exsultet is paraphrased, not quoted (no verified public-domain English text in hand): calls to rejoice; 'this is the night' lines naming the Exodus, the pillar of fire, and Christ breaking the chains of death; the 'happy fault' (felix culpa) line. Confirm the paraphrase.
Claims rule: the outline's 'ancient' is rendered 'old'; no dates or authorship given. Hebrew Bible readings attributed to 'churches that keep the full vigil'.

Lumen Christi / Deo gratias given as 'the light of Christ' / 'thanks be to God'; the threefold singing is not counted. Return of the alleluia attributed to 'churches that set the alleluia aside for Lent'. Baptisms 'some churches'. Confirm.
Jewish Passover mentioned as a neighbor, without comparison; confirm wording.
Original is Latin (haec nox est), ecclesiastical pronunciation; acceptable for this path? Otherwise set to null.
Editor pass: the narrator no longer claims John 1:5 sums up the vigil; it is offered as a line the candle carries.
Second editor pass: 'each line starts the same way' overstated the Exsultet's refrain; now 'line after line'.

Audit pass: 'by that light alone' removed; in the current Roman Missal the church lights may be lit at the third 'Light of Christ', before the Exsultet, and practice varies by church. Keeper: confirm the lighting sequence as described.
